must_remember: The work done by a force field $F$ along a smooth directed curve $C$ is given by the line integral $W = \int_{C} F \cdot dr$.
A force field is conservative if and only if its line integral around any closed loop is identically zero ($\oint_{C} F \cdot dr = 0$).
For conservative forces, the line integral between two points is completely independent of the path taken and depends only on the initial and final positions.
The relationship between a conservative force and its potential energy $U$ is expressed as $F = -\nabla U$, or $U(r_2) - U(r_1) = -\int_{r_1}^{r_2} F \cdot dr$.
Non-conservative forces such as friction dissipate mechanical energy, making their line integrals path-dependent and non-zero for closed loops.
The Coriolis force in rotating frames does zero instantaneous work because it remains perpendicular to the velocity vector ($F \cdot v = 0$).

glossary.meaning: The integration of the tangential component of a vector force field along a directed curve, representing mechanical work.
A force for which work done along a path is independent of the path and depends only on endpoints, with zero closed-loop line integral.
A scalar energy function $U$ whose negative gradient yields the conservative force vector ($F = -\nabla U$).
A force such as friction whose work depends on the path taken and which results in mechanical energy dissipation.
A fictitious force in rotating reference frames that performs zero work since it is always perpendicular to the particle velocity.
A force whose line of action always passes through a fixed center point, directed radially as $f(r) \hat{r}$.
